title: Autophagy in Human Disease: Mechanisms, Pathophysiological Roles, and Translational Opportunities for Prevention, Drug Design, and Therapy

subsections.section_title: Molecular and Cellular Foundations of Autophagy
subsections.content:
Autophagy comprises conserved lysosome-directed pathways that deliver cytoplasmic material for degradation and recycling. The term originally described bulk sequestration of cytoplasm during nutrient deprivation, but is now understood to include mechanistically distinct routes: macroautophagy, microautophagy, and chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA) ref [1], ref [2], ref [3]. In macroautophagy, a phagophore expands into a double-membrane autophagosome that subsequently fuses with lysosomes; microautophagy instead involves direct lysosomal or late endosomal invagination of cargo; CMA translocates soluble proteins bearing KFERQ-like motifs across the lysosomal membrane via LAMP2A and HSC70 ref [3], ref [4], ref [5].

Yeast genetics established the conceptual framework for autophagy by identifying autophagy-related (ATG) genes required for starvation-induced vacuolar delivery, many of which are conserved in mammals ref [6], ref [7]. Current nomenclature also distinguishes nonselective autophagy, which broadly mobilizes intracellular nutrients, from selective autophagy, in which receptors target defined substrates such as mitochondria, protein aggregates, pathogens, peroxisomes, or ER fragments for lysosomal clearance ref [8], ref [9], ref [10]. Related endolysosomal processes, including LC3-associated phagocytosis and other noncanonical ATG8 conjugation pathways, share parts of the autophagy machinery but are not equivalent to canonical macroautophagy because they act on single-membrane compartments and follow distinct upstream rules ref [11], ref [12].

Operationally, autophagy should therefore be defined by pathway, cargo route, and completion of flux rather than by static accumulation of vesicles or LC3 puncta alone ref [13], ref [14]. This distinction is essential because increased autophagosome number may reflect either pathway activation or impaired lysosomal clearance, and because the biological outputs of bulk versus selective autophagy differ across stress adaptation, immunity, and tissue homeostasis ref [14], ref [15], ref [16].

subsections.section_title: Molecular and Cellular Foundations of Autophagy
subsections.content:
Autophagosome biogenesis begins with activation of the ULK1/Atg1 kinase complex, which integrates nutrient and stress signals from mTORC1 and AMPK to initiate phagophore formation at specialized membrane assembly sites ref [17], ref [18], ref [19]. ULK1 then engages the class III phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase complex I, composed of VPS34, VPS15, BECN1 and ATG14L, to generate phosphatidylinositol-3-phosphate and recruit early effectors such as WIPI proteins and DFCP1 that organize the nascent isolation membrane ref [20], ref [21], ref [22], ref [23].

Expansion of the phagophore depends on two ubiquitin-like conjugation systems. The ATG12–ATG5-ATG16L1 complex acts in an E3-like manner to support lipidation of ATG8 family proteins, converting LC3/GABARAP proteins from their cytosolic forms to phosphatidylethanolamine-conjugated membrane species that promote membrane growth, cargo capture and maturation ref [24], ref [25], ref [26], ref [27]. Structural and biochemical studies further place WIPI2 upstream of ATG16L1 recruitment, thereby coupling PI3P production to LC3 lipidation at the growing phagophore ref [28].

Membrane supply for autophagosome formation is multifactorial, involving ER subdomains, ATG9 vesicles and COPII-related trafficking, with ATG2 functioning as a lipid-transfer factor at ER–phagophore contact sites to sustain expansion ref [29], ref [30], ref [31]. Closure and completion of the autophagosome require coordinated remodeling by ATG8 proteins and the ESCRT machinery, after which the sealed double-membrane vesicle becomes competent for fusion with lysosomes ref [32], ref [33]. Together, these modules define a highly ordered assembly pathway whose disruption alters autophagic flux and disease susceptibility.

subsections.section_title: Molecular and Cellular Foundations of Autophagy
subsections.subsection_title: Selective Autophagy and Organelle Quality Control
subsections.content:
Selective autophagy confers cargo specificity on a pathway once viewed as bulk cytoplasmic turnover. This specificity is typically mediated by receptors such as p62/SQSTM1, NBR1, NDP52/CALCOCO2 and optineurin, which recognize ubiquitinated substrates and simultaneously bind ATG8 family proteins through LC3-interacting regions, thereby coupling damaged or superfluous material to nascent autophagosomes ref [34], ref [35], ref [36], ref [37]. More broadly, selective autophagy maintains proteostasis and limits inflammatory signaling by clearing protein aggregates, invading microbes, and dysfunctional organelles ref [38], ref [39].

Mitophagy is the best-characterized organelle quality-control pathway. Loss of mitochondrial membrane potential stabilizes PINK1 on the outer mitochondrial membrane, where it activates and recruits Parkin to amplify ubiquitin signaling on mitochondrial substrates; these ubiquitin chains are then decoded by receptors including optineurin and NDP52 to drive autophagosome formation around damaged mitochondria ref [40], ref [41], ref [42], ref [43]. Parallel receptor-mediated pathways, notably BNIP3, NIX/BNIP3L and FUNDC1, enable context-specific mitophagy during hypoxia, erythroid maturation and developmental remodeling ref [44], ref [45], ref [46].

Other forms of organellophagy extend this surveillance logic to additional compartments. Endoplasmic reticulum turnover (ER-phagy) is mediated by resident receptors such as FAM134B, SEC62 and RTN3 that reshape or mark ER subdomains for lysosomal removal during stress recovery or constitutive remodeling ref [47], ref [48], ref [49]. Lysophagy clears ruptured lysosomes after galectin sensing and ubiquitin deposition, whereas pexophagy eliminates excess or oxidatively damaged peroxisomes, together preserving metabolic fitness and preventing secondary cellular injury ref [50], ref [51]. Thus, selective autophagy integrates damage recognition, membrane remodeling and lysosomal degradation into a core organelle quality-control network.

subsections.section_title: Molecular and Cellular Foundations of Autophagy
subsections.content:
Autophagy is governed by nutrient-, energy-, and stress-sensing pathways that converge on the ULK1 initiation complex and the class III phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase machinery. mTORC1 is the dominant nutrient-responsive brake: under amino acid and growth factor sufficiency it phosphorylates ULK1 and ATG13 to suppress autophagosome biogenesis, whereas starvation-induced mTORC1 inhibition rapidly activates the pathway ref [52], ref [53], ref [54]. In parallel, AMPK couples low energy charge to autophagy by directly activating ULK1 and by inhibiting mTORC1 through TSC2 and RAPTOR phosphorylation ref [18], ref [55], ref [56]. The Beclin 1–VPS34 complex is also regulated by upstream kinases and cofactors, integrating growth factor withdrawal, nutrient stress, and membrane trafficking cues into phagophore nucleation ref [57], ref [58].

Autophagy signaling is further shaped by transcriptional and stress-response networks. TFEB and related MiT/TFE factors coordinate lysosomal and autophagy gene expression and are restrained by mTORC1-dependent phosphorylation; starvation or lysosomal stress promotes their nuclear translocation and sustained catabolic adaptation ref [59], ref [60]. Hypoxia induces autophagy through HIF-dependent transcriptional programs, including BNIP3 and BNIP3L/NIX, which can disrupt inhibitory BCL2–Beclin 1 interactions and favor organelle turnover ref [61], ref [62], ref [63]. Endoplasmic reticulum stress and integrated stress responses also stimulate autophagy via eIF2α-ATF4 signaling and stress-activated kinases such as JNK, linking proteostasis failure to degradative recycling ref [64], ref [65].

Context-dependent crosstalk adds additional regulatory layers. Insulin–PI3K–AKT signaling suppresses autophagy largely through mTORC1, whereas FOXO transcription factors promote expression of autophagy genes during fasting or reduced insulin signaling ref [66], ref [17]. Because these networks operate with strong cell-type and temporal specificity, the same upstream stimulus may either permit basal housekeeping autophagy or drive robust stress-induced flux, a distinction that is central for interpreting autophagy in physiology and disease.

subsections.section_title: Molecular and Cellular Foundations of Autophagy
subsections.content:
Autophagic flux denotes the dynamic rate of cargo sequestration, autophagosome maturation, lysosomal fusion, and intralysosomal degradation, and is therefore more informative than static measurements of autophagosome abundance alone. Early consensus guidelines emphasized that increases in LC3-positive structures or LC3-II can reflect either induction or blockade of downstream steps, necessitating assays that distinguish formation from turnover ref [67], ref [2]. Pharmacologic interruption of lysosomal acidification or fusion with bafilomycin A1, chloroquine, or related agents remains a common strategy to estimate LC3-II turnover, while degradation of the autophagy receptor SQSTM1/p62 provides a complementary but context-dependent readout because its expression is transcriptionally regulated and cargo selective ref [2], ref [68], ref [69].

Fluorescent reporters have greatly improved temporal and spatial assessment of flux. Tandem GFP-mRFP/mCherry-LC3 exploits acid-sensitive GFP quenching in autolysosomes to discriminate autophagosomes from autolysosomes in living cells ref [70], ref [71]. More recently, pH-sensitive probes such as mt-Keima enabled quantitative measurement of selective lysosomal delivery of mitochondria, illustrating how organelle-specific reporters can resolve pathway selectivity that bulk LC3 assays miss ref [72]. Ultrastructural analysis by electron microscopy remains a valuable orthogonal method for identifying double-membrane autophagosomes and degradative intermediates, particularly when integrated with molecular assays ref [67], ref [73].

Because autophagy is highly sensitive to nutrient status, cell type, and lysosomal competence, rigorous experimental design requires multiple orthogonal assays, matched time courses, and careful interpretation of genetic perturbations in ATG genes ref [67], ref [2], ref [74]. In vivo, transgenic fluorescent LC3 and tandem-LC3 reporter mice have facilitated tissue-level flux measurements, while human studies increasingly combine histology, immunoblotting, and lysosomal markers to avoid overinterpreting static snapshots ref [75], ref [76]. Emerging assays based on long-lived protein degradation, flow cytometry, and high-content imaging further support quantitative profiling, but no single method is sufficient across all models ref [77], ref [78], ref [79], ref [80].

subsections.section_title: Autophagy in Host Defense and Infectious Diseases
subsections.subsection_title: Autophagy as an Innate Immune Mechanism
subsections.content:
Autophagy is an evolutionarily conserved arm of innate immunity that captures and degrades cytosolic microbes, damaged organelles, and inflammatory substrates through lysosomal delivery. Genetic studies first linked autophagy proteins to host defense by showing that IRGM and ATG5 regulate resistance to intracellular pathogens, while pattern-recognition and cytokine signals, including Toll-like receptors and IFN-γ, can activate the pathway refs [1–4]. Beyond bulk recycling, selective autophagy targets pathogens or pathogen-containing compartments through ubiquitin-dependent cargo receptors such as p62, NDP52, and optineurin, which couple microbial “eat-me” signals to LC3-positive membranes refs [5–8].

This antimicrobial program, often termed xenophagy, intersects closely with inflammatory signaling. Autophagy proteins promote phagosome maturation, facilitate antigen processing, and limit excessive inflammasome activation by clearing damaged mitochondria and endogenous danger signals refs [9–12]. Importantly, LC3-associated phagocytosis and related noncanonical pathways extend autophagy gene function to single-membrane phagosomes, broadening innate immune control of fungi, bacteria, and dead-cell cargo refs [13,14]. Thus, autophagy is not merely a degradative housekeeping pathway but a multifunctional innate immune module that integrates microbial sensing, vesicular trafficking, and immune homeostasis; defects in these processes help explain the association of ATG16L1, IRGM, and related loci with inflammatory disease susceptibility refs [2,15,16].

subsections.section_title: Autophagy in Host Defense and Infectious Diseases
subsections.content:
Autophagy is a major cell-autonomous defense against intracellular bacteria, coupling microbial sensing to lysosomal destruction. A seminal example is Mycobacterium tuberculosis, for which starvation or IFN-γ induces autophagy and enhances mycobacterial killing in macrophages, linking canonical autophagy to antimycobacterial immunity ref [97]. Genetic studies further connected susceptibility to mycobacterial disease and Crohn’s disease with autophagy regulators such as IRGM and ATG16L1, reinforcing the physiological importance of this pathway in host defense ref [98], ref [99]. Upstream, pattern-recognition and stress pathways including TLR signaling and ubiquitin-dependent danger recognition can mobilize antibacterial autophagy programs ref [100], ref [101].

Selective autophagy (xenophagy) is especially important once bacteria damage or escape pathogen-containing vacuoles. Cytosolic Salmonella are decorated with ubiquitin and recognized by adaptors including p62, NDP52, and optineurin, which connect bacteria to LC3-positive membranes and promote restriction ref [102], ref [87], ref [103]. Similar logic applies to Shigella and Listeria, although these pathogens encode countermeasures: Shigella IcsB masks the bacterial surface from ATG5-dependent recognition, whereas Listeria ActA and InlK reduce autophagic capture by limiting ubiquitin coating or recruiting host factors ref [104], ref [105], ref [106]. Galectin sensing of damaged vacuoles provides an additional trigger for antibacterial targeting, integrating membrane damage with selective autophagy machinery ref [107].

Bacteria also actively subvert autophagy to preserve replicative niches. Legionella pneumophila and Coxiella burnetii intersect with autophagic trafficking to remodel vacuoles, while several pathogens deploy effectors that block autophagosome maturation or lysosomal fusion ref [108], ref [109]. Conversely, autophagy proteins can function in noncanonical pathways such as LC3-associated phagocytosis, which contributes to phagosome maturation and antibacterial activity independently of classical double-membrane autophagosome formation ref [110]. Together, these findings show that intracellular clearance reflects a dynamic competition between host xenophagy and bacterial immune evasion, making autophagy an attractive axis for host-directed therapy in difficult bacterial infections ref [16].

subsections.section_title: Autophagy in Host Defense and Infectious Diseases
subsections.content:
Viruses engage autophagy in highly context-dependent ways, exploiting a pathway that can otherwise contribute to innate restriction, antigen processing, and inflammatory control. Early work with herpesviruses showed direct antagonism of core autophagy machinery: herpes simplex virus type 1 ICP34.5 binds Beclin 1 to suppress autophagosome formation, enhancing neurovirulence, while the gamma-herpesvirus Bcl-2 homologs encoded by Kaposi’s sarcoma-associated herpesvirus and murine gammaherpesvirus 68 similarly inhibit Beclin 1-dependent autophagy ref [111], ref [112], ref [113], ref [114]. These studies established viral blockade of autophagy as a bona fide virulence strategy.

By contrast, several RNA viruses remodel autophagy to support replication. Poliovirus and coronaviruses induce double-membrane vesicles linked to the autophagy machinery, and hepatitis C virus requires autophagic functions for efficient RNA replication and metabolic adaptation ref [115], ref [116], ref [117], ref [118]. Flaviviruses provide a particularly clear example of proviral autophagy: dengue virus triggers lipophagy to mobilize cellular lipids and support replication, while Zika virus proteins inhibit Akt-mTOR signaling to stimulate autophagy and promote vertical transmission-associated pathogenesis ref [119], ref [120]. Enteroviruses can also subvert selective autophagy; coxsackievirus B3 cleaves autophagy receptors to uncouple cargo recognition from degradation and preserve a replication-permissive compartment ref [121].

Other viruses manipulate late autophagic flux rather than initiation. Influenza A virus M2 blocks autophagosome maturation, causing LC3-positive vesicle accumulation, and HIV-1 Nef inhibits autophagic degradation in macrophages, limiting antiviral clearance while preserving steps advantageous for assembly or persistence ref [122], ref [123]. Autophagy can nevertheless retain antiviral functions, including delivery of viral nucleic acids to endosomal sensors in plasmacytoid dendritic cells and support of MHC class II presentation of endogenous viral antigens ref [124], ref [125]. Accordingly, whether autophagy is antiviral or proviral depends on the infected cell type, the stage of flux targeted, and the extent to which viral proteins rewire selective versus bulk autophagy pathways ref [126].

subsections.section_title: Autophagy in Host Defense and Infectious Diseases
subsections.content:
In fungal infection, autophagy shapes both cell-autonomous defense and inflammatory calibration, but its consequences are context dependent. Work on Aspergillus has defined LC3-associated phagocytosis (LAP) as a prominent antifungal pathway downstream of pattern-recognition signaling and NADPH oxidase activity, promoting phagosome maturation and fungal control in macrophages and in vivo ref [127], ref [128], ref [129]. Human genetics further links this axis to disease susceptibility: variants in CLEC7A and autophagy-related pathways have been associated with altered antifungal immunity, while studies in chronic granulomatous disease connect defective ROS production to impaired autophagic handling of Aspergillus and excessive inflammation ref [130], ref [131]. In Candida infection, autophagy proteins also influence phagocyte function and cytokine responses, although the relative contributions of canonical autophagy versus LAP can vary by cell type and fungal morphotype ref [132], ref [133].

Parasitic infections reveal an equally dual role. During Toxoplasma gondii infection, immunity-related GTPases and guanylate-binding proteins are recruited to the parasitophorous vacuole through autophagy-related mechanisms involving ATG proteins, enabling IFN-γ-dependent restriction in murine cells ref [134], ref [135], ref [136]. At the same time, noncanonical functions of autophagy proteins in antigen presentation and cytokine regulation influence adaptive immunity to the parasite ref [137]. In malaria, Plasmodium engages host autophagic machinery in hepatocytes, while parasite proteins can evade or remodel LC3-positive membranes to preserve the replicative niche ref [138], ref [139]. For kinetoplastids, autophagy intersects with both host resistance and parasite survival: Leishmania can exploit host autophagic responses to support intracellular persistence, whereas autophagy stimulation may also enhance antiparasitic effector programs depending on species and host context ref [140], ref [141].

Collectively, fungal and parasitic pathogens underscore that autophagy is not uniformly microbicidal; rather, selective autophagy, LAP, and autophagy-related trafficking can either restrict eukaryotic pathogens or be co-opted to sustain infection. This complexity is also evident in helminth-associated immunity, where autophagy influences barrier responses, granulomatous inflammation, and type 2 immune homeostasis rather than direct pathogen destruction ref [142]. These observations support therapeutic strategies that modulate discrete autophagy modules, rather than globally increasing or suppressing autophagic flux, in invasive mycoses and parasitic disease ref [143].

subsections.section_title: Autophagy in Host Defense and Infectious Diseases
subsections.content:
Autophagy shapes infection-associated immunopathology by coupling pathogen control to restraint of damaging inflammation. A central mechanism is mitophagy-dependent limitation of mitochondrial ROS and mitochondrial DNA release, thereby dampening NLRP3 inflammasome activation and IL-1β/IL-18 production ref [89], ref [144]. Consistent with this, macrophage autophagy proteins also regulate inflammation independently of canonical degradative autophagy, and defects in ATG16L1-linked pathways can amplify endotoxin- or microbiota-driven tissue injury ref [145], ref [146]. In vivo, defective autophagy contributes to exaggerated immunopathology during sepsis, influenza, and inflammatory bowel disease–like states, highlighting that insufficient autophagic flux may be as harmful as inadequate microbial clearance ref [147], ref [148], ref [149].

These insights motivate host-directed therapies that modulate, rather than simply maximize, autophagy. mTOR inhibition enhances antimicrobial autophagy and has shown benefit in experimental mycobacterial and viral infection contexts, although broad immunosuppression remains a concern ref [150], ref [151]. AMPK activators such as metformin can promote autophagy, temper inflammatory injury, and have been associated with improved tuberculosis outcomes in observational and experimental studies ref [152], ref [153]. Vitamin D also induces antimicrobial autophagy through the cathelicidin pathway and may complement conventional antimicrobials ref [154]. More selective strategies include targeting TFEB-dependent lysosomal biogenesis, autophagy-inflammasome crosstalk, or mitophagy checkpoints to preserve tissue tolerance while maintaining host resistance ref [155], ref [156].

Therapeutic translation nonetheless requires context specificity. Some pathogens exploit autophagy-like membranes or late autophagic compartments for replication or persistence, implying that indiscriminate induction may worsen disease in selected viral or intracellular bacterial infections ref [157], ref [158]. Accordingly, the major challenge is to identify stage-, cell type-, and pathogen-specific windows in which autophagy modulation reduces immunopathology without creating a permissive niche, a principle increasingly emphasized in host-directed therapy frameworks for tuberculosis and severe viral disease ref [153], ref [159].

subsections.section_title: Autophagy in Non-Infectious Diseases: Degeneration, Inflammation, and Malignancy
subsections.content:
Neurons are especially dependent on basal autophagy because of their longevity, polarized morphology, and limited regenerative capacity. Genetic disruption of core autophagy machinery in the nervous system causes rapid neurodegeneration with ubiquitin-positive inclusions, establishing autophagy as a constitutive proteostatic safeguard rather than merely a stress response ref [160], ref [161]. Consistently, selective autophagy receptors such as p62/SQSTM1 and NBR1 coordinate the removal of aggregation-prone cargo, while defective autophagosome maturation or lysosomal clearance promotes toxic protein accumulation and axonal pathology ref [38], ref [162].

In Alzheimer’s disease, autophagic vacuoles accumulate prominently in dystrophic neurites, indicating impaired flux, and presenilin-1 dysfunction has been linked to defective lysosomal acidification and autophagy maturation ref [163], ref [164]. In Parkinson’s disease, several familial genes converge on autophagy–lysosome quality control: α-synuclein is normally degraded by chaperone-mediated autophagy, whereas mutant LRRK2 and PINK1/Parkin pathway defects perturb lysosomal function and mitophagy, thereby sensitizing dopaminergic neurons to mitochondrial injury ref [165], ref [166], ref [40], ref [167].

Huntington’s disease and related proteinopathies further illustrate the double-edged role of autophagy. Mutant huntingtin interferes with cargo recognition and autophagosome function, yet pharmacologic or genetic enhancement of autophagy can facilitate clearance of toxic species and improve phenotypes in experimental models ref [168], ref [169]. Similar principles extend to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis/frontotemporal degeneration, where mutations in p62/SQSTM1, optineurin, TBK1, and C9ORF72 disrupt selective autophagy and lysosomal trafficking ref [170], ref [171], ref [172]. Together, these findings support autophagy-restoring strategies, although stage-, cell type-, and compartment-specific defects must be defined to avoid exacerbating stalled degradative intermediates ref [173].

subsections.section_title: Autophagy in Non-Infectious Diseases: Degeneration, Inflammation, and Malignancy
subsections.content:
Autophagy is a central determinant of cardiac adaptation to stress, balancing energy supply, protein/organelle quality control, and cell survival. Basal cardiomyocyte autophagy is required for homeostasis, as genetic disruption of Atg5 causes rapid cardiac hypertrophy, ventricular dilation, and contractile dysfunction, whereas pressure overload induces a marked rise in autophagic flux [1,2]. During ischemia, AMPK-dependent autophagy is generally viewed as protective by sustaining ATP production and limiting damage, but excessive or persistent activation during reperfusion may contribute to cell loss, in part through Beclin 1-dependent mechanisms [3,4]. Consistent with this context dependence, glucose deprivation activates autophagy through AMPK, whereas reperfusion-associated stress can uncouple autophagy from efficient clearance [5].

Mitophagy has emerged as a particularly important cardioprotective arm of the pathway. Mitochondrial quality control mediated by PINK1/Parkin and receptors such as BNIP3 and NIX limits reactive oxygen species accumulation and mitochondrial permeability transition, thereby constraining infarct size and adverse remodeling [6,7,8]. Defects in lysosomal function and autophagosome maturation also influence ischemic vulnerability; impaired flux after ischemia-reperfusion has been linked to reduced clearance capacity, whereas restoration of lysosomal competence improves functional recovery [9,10]. Beyond acute infarction, altered autophagy contributes to chronic heart failure, diabetic cardiomyopathy, and vascular disease, where it may be either adaptive or maladaptive depending on disease stage and stimulus intensity [11,12].

In the vasculature, autophagy modulates endothelial survival, nitric oxide bioavailability, smooth-muscle phenotype, and plaque stability. Protective autophagy restrains inflammation and senescence in atherosclerosis, whereas defective autophagy promotes inflammasome activation, defective efferocytosis, and necrotic core formation [13,14]. Therapeutically, interventions that tune rather than maximally activate autophagy appear most promising; mTOR inhibition, caloric restriction mimetics, and ischemic conditioning can be beneficial experimentally, but the dual nature of autophagy in pressure overload and reperfusion injury argues for cell type-, timing-, and flux-aware targeting [2,4,15,16].

subsections.section_title: Autophagy in Non-Infectious Diseases: Degeneration, Inflammation, and Malignancy
subsections.content:
Autophagy is deeply integrated into inflammatory control because it removes damaged mitochondria, protein aggregates, and inflammasome-activating danger signals while also shaping antigen presentation and lymphocyte survival. Genetic studies first connected this pathway to human inflammatory disease through susceptibility loci in Crohn’s disease, notably ATG16L1 and IRGM, linking defective xenophagy and epithelial stress responses to chronic intestinal inflammation ref [189], ref [190], ref [96]. Experimental work further showed that Atg16L1 restrains endotoxin-induced IL-1β production, providing a mechanistic bridge between impaired autophagy and exaggerated innate immune activation ref [191]. Consistently, autophagy proteins limit inflammasome signaling by promoting mitochondrial quality control and constraining mitochondrial DNA- and ROS-dependent NLRP3 activation ref [89], ref [192].

In barrier tissues and myeloid cells, defective autophagy compromises microbial handling, Paneth-cell secretory programs, and resolution of mucosal inflammation, thereby helping explain the prominent role of autophagy variants in inflammatory bowel disease ref [193], ref [194], ref [195]. Beyond the gut, autophagy intersects broadly with cytokine and interferon circuits in autoimmunity. Beclin 1 and LC3-associated pathways influence phagocytic clearance of dying cells and the presentation of self-antigens, processes relevant to loss of tolerance ref [196], ref [197]. In lupus-prone settings, altered autophagy has been linked to survival and activation of autoreactive B cells and plasma cells, while autophagy inhibition can attenuate disease phenotypes in experimental models ref [198], ref [199].

Autophagy also contributes to the pathogenesis and therapeutic response of rheumatic disease. In rheumatoid arthritis, synovial fibroblasts and osteoclast-lineage cells exploit autophagy for survival under hypoxia and inflammatory stress, potentially sustaining pannus formation and joint destruction ref [200], ref [201]. Conversely, autophagy can support regulatory and anti-inflammatory programs in certain immune compartments, emphasizing strong context dependence. Accordingly, current frameworks view autophagy not simply as anti- or pro-inflammatory, but as a tunable network that can either preserve immune homeostasis or reinforce chronic inflammation depending on cell type, stage of disease, and the balance between canonical autophagy, selective autophagy, and LC3-associated phagocytosis ref [202], ref [133].

subsections.section_title: Autophagy in Non-Infectious Diseases: Degeneration, Inflammation, and Malignancy
subsections.content:
Autophagy is a central effector of metabolic adaptation, coupling nutrient sensing to organelle quality control and substrate mobilization. Genetic evidence from liver, adipose tissue, pancreatic islets, and hypothalamus shows that disruption of core autophagy genes perturbs glucose homeostasis, lipid turnover, and endocrine signaling rather than simply causing nonspecific cellular stress ref [161], ref [203], ref [204], ref [205]. In obesity and insulin resistance, defective autophagic flux has been linked to endoplasmic reticulum stress and impaired insulin action, whereas nutrient excess can suppress autophagy through chronic mTORC1 activation ref [206], ref [207], ref [208].

A particularly important theme is selective autophagy of lipid droplets and mitochondria. Hepatic autophagy promotes lipophagy, thereby limiting triglyceride accumulation and steatosis ref [209], ref [210]. Conversely, autophagy deficiency in adipocytes alters differentiation and favors a metabolically abnormal fat phenotype, while adipose Atg7 loss in mice increases insulin sensitivity despite severe defects in white adipose tissue development, underscoring marked tissue- and context-dependence ref [203], ref [211]. In pancreatic β cells, basal autophagy preserves organelle integrity and insulin secretory capacity; β-cell-specific Atg7 deletion causes degeneration and hyperglycemia, and human type 2 diabetic islets display accumulation of autophagic vacuoles consistent with impaired flux ref [204], ref [212].

Endocrine control of whole-body energy balance is also strongly shaped by neuronal autophagy. Loss of Atg7 in AgRP neurons reduces food intake and adiposity, whereas hypothalamic autophagy broadly participates in fasting responses and neuropeptide mobilization ref [205], ref [213]. Beyond diabetes and obesity, lysosomal-autophagic dysfunction contributes to inherited metabolic disease, exemplified by Pompe disease, in which defective glycogen clearance is compounded by autophagic buildup in muscle ref [214], ref [215]. Therapeutically, autophagy modulation remains double-edged: caloric restriction and AMPK activation can improve metabolic phenotypes partly through autophagy induction, yet excessive or incomplete autophagy may aggravate lipotoxicity, β-cell failure, or endocrine stress responses ref [216], ref [217].

subsections.section_title: Autophagy in Non-Infectious Diseases: Degeneration, Inflammation, and Malignancy
subsections.subsection_title: Cancer Biology and Tumor Context Dependence
subsections.content:
Autophagy has a strongly context-dependent role in cancer, acting as a barrier to transformation in some settings while supporting survival of established tumors under metabolic, oxidative, and therapeutic stress. Early genetic evidence for tumor suppression came from monoallelic loss of BECN1 in human breast and ovarian cancers and from Beclin 1-deficient mice, which develop increased spontaneous malignancies, implicating basal autophagy in genome protection and tissue homeostasis ref [218], ref [219]. Mechanistically, defective autophagy promotes damaged mitochondria, reactive oxygen species, DNA damage, and chronic inflammation; loss of core autophagy genes such as Atg5 or Atg7 can accelerate benign liver tumorigenesis, partly through p62/SQSTM1 accumulation and oxidative stress signaling ref [220], ref [221], ref [222].

In contrast, many advanced cancers become autophagy-dependent. Ras-driven models demonstrated that autophagy sustains mitochondrial metabolism, tricarboxylic acid cycle intermediates, and survival during nutrient limitation ref [223], ref [224]. Genetic ablation of Atg7 impairs progression of Kras-driven lung tumors and alters fate toward oncocytoma-like lesions, while pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma and other hard-wired metabolic tumors show marked reliance on lysosomal-autophagic flux ref [225], ref [226], ref [227]. Tumor-extrinsic autophagy also contributes: stromal and systemic autophagy can provide metabolites such as alanine or arginine to support tumor growth in nutrient-poor microenvironments ref [228], ref [229].

These dual activities explain why therapeutic targeting remains nuanced. Autophagy can mediate resistance to chemotherapy, targeted kinase inhibitors, endocrine therapy, and radiotherapy, yet in selected contexts excessive or dysregulated autophagy may contribute to cell death ref [230], ref [231]. Clinically, lysosomal inhibitors such as hydroxychloroquine have been combined with cytotoxic or targeted agents, but variable pharmacodynamic inhibition and biomarker uncertainty have limited broad efficacy ref [232], ref [233]. Current strategies therefore emphasize genotype-, lineage-, and microenvironment-informed deployment of autophagy modulation, including more potent lysosomal inhibitors and direct ULK1/VPS34 pathway targeting ref [234].

subsections.section_title: Autophagy in Lifestyle-Related Disorders and Preventive Health
subsections.content:
Nutritional state is a dominant regulator of autophagy, linking dietary patterns to metabolic resilience. Mechanistically, amino acids, insulin, and growth factors suppress autophagy through mTORC1, whereas nutrient scarcity activates AMPK–ULK1 signaling and lysosomal catabolism; these principles were established in yeast and mammalian systems and remain central to preventive medicine models of dietary intervention ref [208], ref [18], ref [235], ref [24]. Beyond total caloric load, nutrient quality also matters: leucine and other amino acids potently restrain autophagic flux, while excess lipid availability, glucolipotoxicity, and chronic overnutrition can impair autophagy and thereby worsen insulin resistance, steatosis, and cardiometabolic risk ref [236], ref [237], ref [238].

Fasting and caloric restriction are therefore among the best-studied physiological inducers of autophagy. In mammals, starvation rapidly induces autophagy in liver and other tissues ref [239], while caloric restriction extends lifespan in model organisms partly through autophagy-dependent stress adaptation ref [240], ref [241], ref [242]. Genetic studies further support a causal role: autophagy genes are required for the lifespan benefits of caloric restriction or nutrient-signaling attenuation in C. elegans and other systems ref [243], ref [244]. In humans, direct tissue-level evidence remains limited, but intermittent fasting and energy restriction improve weight, insulin sensitivity, blood pressure, and inflammatory markers, outcomes consistent with enhanced metabolic housekeeping and organelle quality control ref [245], ref [246].

Translationally, the challenge is to distinguish beneficial, pulsatile autophagy induction from malnutrition or frailty-promoting undernutrition. Time-restricted feeding and fasting-mimicking diets may offer more feasible strategies than chronic severe caloric restriction, potentially recapitulating nutrient-sensing reprogramming with better adherence and safety ref [247], ref [248]. Future preventive frameworks should integrate dietary composition, fasting periodicity, age, and baseline metabolic state, as the health impact of autophagy activation is likely context dependent rather than uniformly beneficial.

subsections.section_title: Autophagy in Lifestyle-Related Disorders and Preventive Health
subsections.content:
Physical activity is a potent physiological inducer of autophagy, particularly in skeletal muscle, heart, liver, adipose tissue, and the brain. Acute exercise activates AMPK-ULK1 signaling and suppresses mTORC1, thereby promoting autophagosome formation and lysosomal flux under conditions of energetic stress ref [18], ref [208], ref [249]. A seminal genetic study showed that disruption of exercise-induced BCL2-regulated autophagy impairs endurance capacity and blunts exercise-mediated improvements in glucose homeostasis, supporting a causal role for autophagy in systemic metabolic adaptation ref [250]. In human skeletal muscle, both endurance-type and high-intensity exercise alter LC3, p62/SQSTM1, and lysosomal markers, although interpretation depends on timing, training status, and flux assessment rather than static protein abundance alone ref [251], ref [252], ref [253].

Exercise-induced autophagy also contributes to organelle quality control. Mitophagy and mitochondrial remodeling are coordinated through PGC-1alpha-dependent and Parkin/PINK1-associated programs, helping maintain oxidative capacity and insulin sensitivity during repeated training bouts ref [254], ref [255], ref [256]. In the cardiovascular system, exercise can enhance basal autophagic housekeeping and protect against ischemic or pressure-overload stress, whereas excessive or exhaustive loading may produce maladaptive responses if recovery is inadequate ref [257], ref [258]. In the central nervous system, running and other aerobic paradigms have been linked to increased autophagic flux and improved proteostasis, neurogenesis, and resilience to neurodegenerative stressors in experimental models ref [259], ref [260].

From a preventive-health perspective, exercise appears to restore defective autophagy associated with obesity, insulin resistance, and aging, thereby complementing dietary strategies aimed at metabolic risk reduction ref [250], ref [256], ref [261]. Nonetheless, exercise modality, intensity, duration, and circadian timing likely shape autophagic outputs, and overtraining or prolonged inactivity between bouts may attenuate benefit ref [252], ref [262]. Future work should prioritize standardized human flux measurements and define how individualized exercise prescriptions can harness autophagy without provoking catabolic excess ref [253], ref [2].

subsections.section_title: Autophagy in Lifestyle-Related Disorders and Preventive Health
subsections.subsection_title: Obesity, Sedentary Behavior, and Lifestyle Dysregulation
subsections.content:
Obesity is consistently associated with impaired autophagic flux in metabolically active tissues, linking nutrient excess to insulin resistance, steatosis, and adipose inflammation. In liver, obesity-related suppression of autophagy contributes to endoplasmic reticulum stress and defective lipid turnover, whereas restoration of Atg7-dependent autophagy improves metabolic homeostasis in experimental models ref [263], ref [209]. In adipose tissue, autophagy also shapes adipocyte differentiation and function; genetic disruption of core autophagy genes alters white adipose development and can promote a brown-fat-like phenotype with distinct systemic metabolic consequences ref [264], ref [265]. Human obesity likewise shows lysosomal/autophagic abnormalities in adipose depots, supporting translational relevance ref [266].

Lifestyle dysregulation amplifies these defects. Chronic overnutrition activates mTORC1 and restrains catabolic quality-control pathways, while lipotoxicity and inflammatory signaling further uncouple autophagosome formation from lysosomal clearance ref [208], ref [267]. Sedentary behavior removes an important physiological stimulus for autophagy induction: exercise activates BCL2-regulated autophagy and is required for normal glucose handling during physical activity ref [268], while endurance training and habitual activity improve markers of mitochondrial quality control in metabolic tissues ref [269], ref [270]. Conversely, physical inactivity and prolonged sitting are independently associated with higher cardiometabolic risk, likely in part through failure to engage these protective stress-response pathways ref [271], ref [272].

Sleep and circadian disruption, common in modern obesogenic lifestyles, further perturb autophagy by desynchronizing nutrient sensing, proteostasis, and organelle turnover. Autophagy is under circadian control, and clock disruption impairs metabolic regulation in peripheral tissues ref [273], ref [274]. Obstructive sleep apnea and intermittent hypoxia, frequent in obesity, additionally modulate autophagy and may contribute to adipose dysfunction and systemic insulin resistance ref [275], ref [276]. Together, these observations position autophagy as a mechanistic integrator of obesity, inactivity, and behavioral dysregulation, and a potential target for combined lifestyle interventions.

subsections.section_title: Autophagy in Lifestyle-Related Disorders and Preventive Health
subsections.content:
Aging is accompanied by a progressive decline in basal and inducible autophagy, reducing proteostasis, organelle quality control, and stress adaptation across tissues. Genetic studies in short-lived models first established autophagy as a longevity mechanism: lifespan extension by dietary restriction, reduced insulin/IGF signaling, or TOR inhibition requires intact autophagy machinery in Caenorhabditis elegans and Drosophila ref [1], ref [2], ref [3], ref [4]. In mammals, autophagic flux decreases with age in liver, muscle, brain, and immune compartments, contributing to accumulation of damaged mitochondria, protein aggregates, and chronic inflammation ref [5], ref [6]. These changes link impaired autophagy to frailty, neurodegeneration, metabolic dysfunction, and reduced resilience rather than to lifespan alone.

Conversely, maintaining or restoring autophagy can extend healthspan. Pharmacologic or genetic inhibition of mTOR promotes longevity in multiple species and is associated with increased autophagy ref [7], ref [8]. Tissue-specific enhancement of autophagy is sufficient to improve late-life function in some contexts, while systemic defects accelerate aging phenotypes ref [9], ref [10]. Selective forms such as mitophagy are especially relevant, because mitochondrial dysfunction is a central hallmark of aging; mitophagy regulators including PINK1/Parkin and receptor-mediated pathways influence stem-cell maintenance, muscle fitness, and inflammaging ref [11], ref [12]. Human studies remain more associative, but age-related declines in autophagy markers and lysosomal competence are increasingly documented in sarcopenia, immune senescence, and neurodegenerative disease ref [13], ref [14].

From a preventive-health perspective, autophagy is best viewed as a modifiable node linking healthy lifespan to lifestyle and geroscience interventions. Caloric restriction and some caloric-restriction mimetics induce autophagy and delay age-associated pathology, although chronic overactivation may be context-dependent and tissue specific ref [15], ref [16]. Accordingly, strategies that preserve circadian alignment, metabolic flexibility, and lysosomal function may support healthy aging by sustaining autophagic competence rather than merely maximizing autophagy intensity ref [17].

subsections.section_title: Autophagy in Lifestyle-Related Disorders and Preventive Health
subsections.content:
Beyond diet and exercise, multiple environmental and behavioral exposures modulate autophagy and thereby shape metabolic resilience. Circadian timing is a central regulator: core clock machinery rhythmically controls autophagy gene expression and flux, while autophagy also feeds back on clock function, linking sleep disruption and shift work to impaired cellular quality control and cardiometabolic risk ref [277], ref [278]. In experimental models, sleep fragmentation or deprivation activates stress pathways but can dysregulate effective autophagic clearance, particularly in brain and liver, suggesting that chronic sleep loss may convert adaptive autophagy into maladaptive proteostatic stress ref [279], ref [280].

Psychological and environmental stressors also intersect with autophagy. Oxidative stress, hypoxia, and endoplasmic-reticulum stress engage autophagic programs through AMPK, HIF, and unfolded-protein-response signaling, often with initially protective effects ref [281], ref [18], ref [282]. However, persistent exposure to airborne particulate matter, cigarette smoke, and toxic metals can provoke defective or excessive autophagy, contributing to inflammation, epithelial injury, vascular dysfunction, and insulin resistance ref [283], ref [284], ref [285], ref [286]. Similar concerns extend to endocrine-disrupting chemicals and obesogens, which reprogram lipid handling and autophagy-related pathways in liver and adipose tissue ref [287], ref [288].

These observations support a preventive-health view of autophagy as environmentally plastic. Behavioral regularity, especially stable sleep-wake schedules and light exposure, may help preserve circadian autophagy, whereas reducing pollution and smoking exposure may limit autophagy-linked tissue damage ref [278], ref [284], ref [285]. At the same time, hormetic stimuli such as thermal stress can beneficially engage autophagy and stress resistance when appropriately dosed, highlighting the importance of exposure intensity, duration, and context in determining whether autophagy supports adaptation or disease ref [289], ref [290].

subsections.section_title: Translational Applications: Biomarkers, Drug Design, and Therapeutic Modulation of Autophagy
subsections.content:
Autophagy is an attractive therapeutic target because it sits at the intersection of proteostasis, bioenergetics, immunity, and stress adaptation. Core mechanistic studies established that mTORC1 suppresses autophagy whereas AMPK and the ULK1 complex promote it, creating druggable nodes that integrate nutrient and damage signals [1,2,3]. Genetic dissection of the Atg machinery further showed that autophagosome biogenesis depends on conserved ubiquitin-like conjugation systems and Beclin 1–VPS34 signaling, thereby defining actionable steps for either induction or inhibition [4,5,6].

Therapeutic intent, however, is context dependent. In cancer, autophagy can suppress tumor initiation by limiting genome damage and p62 accumulation, yet established tumors often exploit autophagy to survive hypoxia, metabolic stress, and therapy, motivating both pro- and anti-autophagy strategies [7,8,9,10]. In contrast, augmenting autophagic flux is broadly viewed as beneficial in neurodegeneration and some proteinopathies, where enhanced clearance of toxic aggregates or damaged mitochondria can be protective; rapamycin and trehalose provided early proof of principle in models of Huntington disease and related disorders [11,12,13].

Translation therefore requires matching mechanism to disease state, cell type, and treatment window. Lysosomal inhibitors such as chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine remain the most clinically deployed autophagy blockers, but their pleiotropy and incomplete pathway suppression highlight the need for more selective agents [14,15]. Conversely, activating TFEB-mediated lysosomal biogenesis or restoring mitophagy may offer disease-modifying benefit in disorders marked by impaired degradative capacity [16,17]. Overall, autophagy should be considered less a uniformly beneficial pathway than a conditional vulnerability or resilience program whose therapeutic value depends on precise biological context.

subsections.section_title: Translational Applications: Biomarkers, Drug Design, and Therapeutic Modulation of Autophagy
subsections.content:
Small-molecule control of autophagy has become a pragmatic translational strategy because the pathway can be pharmacologically manipulated at multiple levels, from nutrient sensing and kinase signaling to lysosomal acidification and vesicle maturation. Canonical inducers include mTOR inhibitors such as rapamycin, which first established pharmacologic derepression of autophagy, and ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitors that more completely suppress mTORC1/2 signaling ref [305], ref [306]. AMPK activators and energy-stress mimetics, including metformin and AICAR, also promote autophagy through ULK1-centered signaling and metabolic rewiring ref [307], ref [308]. Additional compounds, such as trehalose, have been explored as mTOR-independent enhancers of autophagic clearance in proteotoxic settings ref [299].

Drug repurposing has been especially attractive because many approved agents already intersect lysosomal or stress-response biology. Chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine remain the most widely deployed clinical autophagy inhibitors, blocking lysosomal acidification and autophagosome degradation, although their pleiotropic effects complicate interpretation ref [309], ref [232]. Other repurposed or clinically familiar compounds include chlorpromazine, verteporfin, and certain cardiac glycosides, which modulate autophagy or autophagy-related trafficking in context-dependent ways ref [310], ref [311], ref [312]. In oncology, these agents are commonly used to test whether tumors are autophagy-addicted under hypoxia, therapy-induced stress, or oncogene activation, but the same drug class may either sensitize or protect cells depending on whether autophagy is cytoprotective, cytostatic, or required for immunogenic death ref [313], ref [230].

A central challenge is that many “autophagy modulators” lack pathway selectivity, motivating efforts to develop compounds against VPS34, ULK1, and lysosomal regulators with more defined mechanisms. Selective VPS34 inhibitors such as SAR405 and PIK-III, and ULK1 inhibitors including SBI-0206965, have strengthened causal interrogation and may enable sharper therapeutic windows than lysosomotropic drugs ref [314], ref [315], ref [316]. Yet successful translation will require pharmacodynamic biomarkers of flux, rational scheduling, and disease-specific deployment, since durable benefit is likely to depend on whether treatment aims to stimulate aggregate/organelle clearance in degenerative disease or to suppress stress adaptation in cancer ref [317], ref [318].

subsections.section_title: Translational Applications: Biomarkers, Drug Design, and Therapeutic Modulation of Autophagy
subsections.subsection_title: Biologics, Nanomedicine, and Targeted Delivery Approaches
subsections.content:
Biologics and gene-based interventions offer a route to manipulate autophagy with greater pathway selectivity than broadly acting small molecules. Early proof-of-concept came from peptide and protein reagents that disrupt the inhibitory BCL2–BECN1 interaction and thereby induce autophagy, establishing a template for mechanism-guided biologic design ref [319], ref [320]. In parallel, viral and non-viral delivery of autophagy genes such as TFEB has shown therapeutic potential by enhancing lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic clearance in models of neurodegeneration and storage disease ref [321], ref [322]. Antibody- and ligand-based biologics can also modulate upstream nutrient-sensing or inflammatory circuits that secondarily reshape autophagic flux, although target engagement must be interpreted in a tissue- and disease-specific manner.

Nanomedicine seeks to overcome the poor pharmacokinetics, systemic toxicity, and limited tissue penetration of autophagy modulators. Nanoparticles, liposomes, micelles, and inorganic carriers can concentrate drugs in tumors or diseased organs, enable co-delivery of autophagy inhibitors with chemotherapeutics, and support stimuli-responsive release in acidic, hypoxic, or redox-active microenvironments ref [323], ref [324], ref [325]. This is particularly relevant in cancer, where lysosomotropic inhibitors such as hydroxychloroquine have modest single-agent activity but may benefit from targeted accumulation and combination scheduling ref [232], ref [326]. Nanocarriers themselves may, however, perturb endo-lysosomal trafficking and autophagy, as shown for several cationic and inorganic formulations, necessitating careful disentangling of carrier effects from cargo effects ref [327], ref [328], ref [329].

Targeted delivery approaches are increasingly integrated with precision medicine. Surface engineering with antibodies, peptides, aptamers, or cell-membrane coatings can enhance uptake by defined cell populations, while organelle-targeted systems direct cargo to lysosomes or mitochondria to rewire selective autophagy pathways ref [330], ref [331]. Nucleic-acid delivery platforms, including lipid nanoparticles and exosome-inspired vesicles, further expand the repertoire to siRNA, mRNA, and CRISPR payloads against ATG regulators or lysosomal genes ref [332], ref [333]. The central translational challenge is to balance potency with context dependence: autophagy may be protective in one compartment yet pathogenic in another, so delivery specificity, pharmacodynamic biomarkers, and longitudinal flux measurements are essential for successful clinical deployment ref [334].

subsections.section_title: Translational Applications: Biomarkers, Drug Design, and Therapeutic Modulation of Autophagy
subsections.content:
Clinical translation of autophagy modulation requires biomarkers that distinguish autophagy induction from blockade and capture the pathway’s dynamic flux rather than static vesicle abundance. Common tissue markers such as LC3B puncta and SQSTM1/p62 are informative but can be misleading when used alone, because increased LC3-II may reflect either enhanced autophagosome biogenesis or impaired lysosomal clearance, while p62 accumulation is context dependent [1,2]. Accordingly, consensus guidance has emphasized multiplexed readouts, including lysosomal markers, electron microscopy, and flux-sensitive assays in paired baseline/on-treatment samples [3,4].

For patient stratification, genomics and expression profiling can identify tumors or tissues with autophagy dependence, including pancreatic cancers driven by KRAS signaling and oxidative stress programs, and settings with allelic loss of core autophagy regulators such as BECN1 [5,6]. Systemic and liquid-biopsy biomarkers are also emerging: circulating LC3-positive extracellular vesicles and secreted autophagy-related proteins have shown pharmacodynamic potential, while lysosomal and metabolic signatures may report target engagement in vivo [7,8]. In lysosomal storage and neurodegenerative disorders, CSF and blood markers linked to autophagic-lysosomal dysfunction, including p62, LAMP-related proteins, and disease-specific cargoes, may help define responsive subgroups [9,10].

Therapy-facing biomarker strategies increasingly integrate pathology, omics, and functional imaging. Hydroxychloroquine trials highlighted the need for direct intratumoral pharmacodynamic assays because peripheral blood mononuclear cell changes correlate imperfectly with tumor autophagy inhibition [11,12]. PET tracers of metabolism, transcriptional signatures of TFEB/lysosomal activation, and spatial analyses of stromal versus tumor-cell autophagy may further refine enrollment for combination regimens [13,14]. More broadly, stratification should account for autophagy’s context specificity in immunity and cell death, since the same biomarker pattern may predict benefit in one disease setting but toxicity or resistance in another [15,16].

subsections.section_title: Translational Applications: Biomarkers, Drug Design, and Therapeutic Modulation of Autophagy
subsections.content:
Clinical translation of autophagy modulation increasingly centers on combination therapy, because autophagy often acts as an adaptive survival response to cytotoxic stress. Preclinical studies showed that chemotherapy, kinase inhibition, proteasome blockade, endocrine therapy, and radiotherapy can induce protective autophagy, creating a rationale for pairing standard agents with lysosomal inhibitors or more selective pathway-directed compounds ref [345], ref [346], ref [347], ref [230]. This framework has been especially influential in RAS-driven tumors, where dependence on autophagy may enhance vulnerability to combined MAPK-pathway and autophagy inhibition ref [348], ref [349].

Early clinical efforts have mainly used hydroxychloroquine or chloroquine to block late-stage autophagy in combination regimens. Phase I/II studies combined hydroxychloroquine with temozolomide and radiation in glioblastoma, with vorinostat in solid tumors, with bortezomib in myeloma, and with gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel or ERK inhibition in pancreatic cancer, demonstrating feasibility but also variable pharmacodynamic inhibition and modest efficacy signals ref [350], ref [232], ref [351], ref [352], ref [353]. Trials in BRAF-mutant glioma and pancreatic cancer further illustrate that context, dosing, and on-target confirmation critically shape outcomes ref [354], ref [355].

Current priorities are therefore translational rather than purely empirical: selecting tumors with demonstrable autophagy dependence, integrating longitudinal biomarkers of flux, and choosing combinations in which autophagy is mechanistically linked to resistance rather than merely stress-associated ref [356], ref [14]. More potent lysosomal agents and upstream inhibitors targeting ULK1 or VPS34 may improve therapeutic index, but clinical success will likely require schedule optimization, toxicity-aware combinations, and biomarker-guided patient enrichment ref [302], ref [357].

subsections.section_title: Translational Applications: Biomarkers, Drug Design, and Therapeutic Modulation of Autophagy
subsections.content:
A central safety challenge in autophagy-directed therapy is that the pathway is homeostatic, pleiotropic, and highly context dependent. Genetic studies established that basal autophagy is indispensable for tissue quality control, neuronal integrity, liver function, and survival during metabolic stress, implying that sustained systemic inhibition may produce cumulative toxicity, whereas excessive activation can promote cell death or cachectic adaptation in selected settings ref [358], ref [161], ref [160], ref [359]. This duality is reinforced in cancer, where autophagy can suppress early tumorigenesis yet support established tumors exposed to hypoxia, nutrient limitation, and therapy-induced stress ref [220], ref [360], ref [361].

Clinical translation is further limited by the pharmacology and assayability of available agents. Widely used lysosomotropic drugs such as chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine incompletely and nonspecifically block autophagic flux, alter endolysosomal pH, and have dose-limiting toxicities including retinopathy, myopathy, cardiomyopathy, and QT prolongation; moreover, trial experience has shown variable intratumoral target inhibition and uncertain exposure-response relationships ref [362], ref [232], ref [363], ref [364]. Even with newer ULK1 or VPS34 inhibitors, on-target liabilities are plausible because these kinases regulate vesicular trafficking, immunity, and metabolic adaptation beyond canonical autophagy ref [365], ref [366].

A major conceptual limitation is that static biomarkers often fail to distinguish autophagosome accumulation from productive flux. Consensus guidelines therefore recommend multimodal, dynamic assessment of LC3, SQSTM1/p62, lysosomal function, and cargo turnover before attributing efficacy or resistance to autophagy modulation ref [2], ref [367]. Patient selection should also account for genotype, lineage, immune state, and treatment context, since autophagy shapes antigen presentation, inflammation, host defense, and therapy responses in opposite directions across diseases ref [202], ref [368]. Overall, safe deployment will likely require intermittent dosing, tissue-targeted delivery, and pharmacodynamic biomarkers that confirm mechanism engagement in the relevant cellular compartment.

subsections.section_title: Emerging Concepts, Knowledge Gaps, and Future Directions
subsections.content:
A central unresolved issue is that autophagy is not a uniformly protective pathway, but a context-dependent stress program whose consequences vary with cell identity, disease stage, and the balance between cargo quality control and bioenergetic support. Foundational genetic studies established autophagy as essential for neonatal adaptation, tissue homeostasis, and aggregate or organelle clearance, yet they also revealed marked tissue specificity in phenotypic outcome ref [161], ref [369], ref [370], ref [371]. This complexity is amplified by selective autophagy modules, including mitophagy and aggrephagy, whose disruption can dominate pathology in some settings while being dispensable in others ref [167], ref [38], ref [372].

Disease biology further illustrates this duality. In neurodegeneration, impaired lysosomal-autophagic flux contributes to toxic protein accumulation and defective organelle turnover, as shown in Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, and lysosomal storage disorders ref [173], ref [373], ref [374], ref [375]. In cancer, however, autophagy can suppress malignant transformation through genome-protective housekeeping yet later sustain established tumors under metabolic and therapeutic stress, producing stage- and genotype-specific liabilities ref [220], ref [226], ref [376]. Similarly, in infection and inflammation, autophagy may restrict intracellular pathogens and tune inflammasome signaling, but some microbes exploit autophagy-related membranes or evade lysosomal destruction ref [39], ref [89].

Future work should therefore move beyond binary models of "more" versus "less" autophagy and instead define disease-relevant flux states, cargo selectivity, and cell-type-specific thresholds for benefit or harm. Integrating spatially resolved measurements with longitudinal perturbation studies will be essential to distinguish adaptive autophagy, maladaptive persistence, and lysosomal failure in specific clinical contexts ref [376], ref [14].

subsections.section_title: Emerging Concepts, Knowledge Gaps, and Future Directions
subsections.content:
Systems-level analyses are reshaping autophagy research by moving beyond single-gene models toward network architectures that link nutrient sensing, organelle quality control, immunity, and cell-fate decisions. Foundational interaction mapping identified an extensive autophagy interactome centered on ATG proteins and trafficking regulators, providing a scaffold for integrative modeling ref [377]. Subsequent transcriptomic and epigenomic studies further showed that lysosomal and autophagy programs are coordinated through MiT/TFE-dependent gene networks responsive to nutrient status and stress ref [378], ref [379]. In parallel, phosphoproteomic analyses established autophagy as a dynamically rewired signaling state downstream of MTOR, AMPK, and selective autophagy receptors rather than a linear pathway ref [380], ref [381].

A major future priority is to integrate multi-omic layers with direct flux measurements. Proteome-wide studies of lysosomal composition and cargo turnover have begun to distinguish transcriptional induction from effective degradation, a distinction often obscured in bulk assays ref [382], ref [383]. Quantitative approaches such as LysoIP-enabled lysosomal metabolomics and organelle-resolved proteomics reveal how autophagy intersects with amino acid homeostasis, mitochondrial metabolism, and lipid remodeling ref [384], ref [385]. Complementary CRISPR screens have uncovered context-specific regulators of selective autophagy, lysophagy, and mitophagy, underscoring that pathway dependencies vary across cell states and stresses ref [386], ref [387], ref [388].

Single-cell and spatial multi-omics now offer a route to resolve this heterogeneity in vivo. Cell atlas studies indicate marked tissue-specific variation in lysosomal and stress-response programs, implying that autophagy competence is embedded in differentiated cell identity ref [389], ref [390]. More broadly, cross-modal frameworks combining transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, and imaging are needed to infer autophagic flux, substrate selectivity, and signaling feedback in disease progression and therapeutic response ref [391], ref [392]. The next challenge is to convert these high-dimensional datasets into predictive, experimentally testable models that capture temporal causality rather than static correlation ref [393].

subsections.section_title: Emerging Concepts, Knowledge Gaps, and Future Directions
subsections.content:
A major frontier is to move beyond cell-autonomous models of autophagy and define how tissue-selective programs are coordinated at organismal scale. Genetic studies in mice established that basal autophagy in liver, brain, skeletal muscle, adipose tissue, pancreatic β cells, and hematopoietic compartments has nonredundant systemic consequences, including altered glucose homeostasis, neuroendocrine stress responses, and inflammatory tone (ref [160], ref [161], ref [394], ref [210], ref [395], ref [396]). Fasting-induced autophagy in peripheral tissues is also integrated by endocrine signals such as glucagon and FGF21, linking nutrient sensing to adaptive remodeling across organs (ref [397], ref [398], ref [399]).

Interorgan communication may occur through several autophagy-dependent routes: regulated secretion, extracellular vesicles, metabolite exchange, and immune signaling. Secretory autophagy can export leaderless cargos and thereby reshape local and systemic cytokine environments (ref [400], ref [401]), while defective autophagy in macrophages and other immune cells amplifies inflammasome activity and propagates sterile inflammation to distal tissues (ref [402], ref [403]). Autophagy in adipocytes and hepatocytes further influences circulating lipid species, ketone production, and hepatokine/adipokine output, suggesting that disease phenotypes often reflect network-level compensation rather than a single-organ defect (ref [210], ref [398], ref [404]).

Future work should map these axes with temporally resolved multi-organ perturbation studies, circulating biomarker analysis, and cell-state-aware spatial atlases. Particularly important questions are whether mitophagy or lysophagy generate distinct endocrine signatures, how microbiota-derived signals intersect with host autophagy to affect whole-body metabolism, and whether tissue-targeted modulation can improve one organ without imposing hidden liabilities elsewhere (ref [405], ref [406], ref [407]).

subsections.section_title: Emerging Concepts, Knowledge Gaps, and Future Directions
subsections.content:
Progress in autophagy research will depend on model systems that preserve physiological context while enabling quantitative perturbation. Foundational genetic studies in yeast and mice established core machinery and in vivo relevance, but they also underscored how nutrient state, developmental stage, and cell identity reshape autophagic outputs ref [24], ref [408], ref [161]. New reporter platforms, including tandem fluorescent LC3 and mitophagy-specific probes such as mt-Keima and mito-QC, have made flux measurements in intact tissues more feasible, helping to distinguish induction from lysosomal blockade and to map pathway activity across organs ref [409], ref [410], ref [411].

A major priority is to move beyond immortalized cell lines toward organoids, assembloids, zebrafish, and human iPSC-derived systems that capture tissue architecture, immune interactions, and patient-specific genetic backgrounds. Human brain organoids have already revealed selective-vulnerability phenotypes relevant to neurodegeneration, while single-cell perturbation strategies now permit parallel analysis of autophagy regulators across diverse cell states ref [412], ref [413], ref [414]. Complementary in vivo CRISPR approaches and proximity-labeling proteomics should further refine organ-specific autophagy networks and cargo selectivity under physiological stress ref [415], ref [416].

Experimental innovation must also address long-standing measurement problems. Consensus guidelines emphasize that static markers alone are insufficient, and recent correlative workflows combining live imaging, electron microscopy, spatial omics, and lysosome functional assays offer a path toward more rigorous inference ref [14], ref [417]. Future models should integrate microphysiological systems, aging paradigms, and microbiome-informed exposures, allowing autophagy to be studied as a dynamic component of multicellular homeostasis rather than an isolated intracellular pathway ref [418], ref [419], ref [420].

subsections.section_title: Emerging Concepts, Knowledge Gaps, and Future Directions
subsections.content:
A preventive and precision-medicine framework for autophagy will require moving beyond the simplistic assumption that more autophagy is uniformly beneficial. Lifespan studies in model organisms established autophagy as a major effector of dietary restriction, mTOR inhibition, and longevity assurance pathways, but they also highlighted strong dependence on age, tissue, and genetic background ref [421], ref [422], ref [423], ref [424]. Human genetics further indicates that autophagy-related risk is disease- and cell-type-specific, as illustrated by ATG16L1 and IRGM in Crohn’s disease and by lysosomal-autophagic defects in neurodegeneration ref [425], ref [426], ref [427], ref [428]. These observations argue for biomarker-guided stratification rather than empiric pathway activation.

Near-term precision strategies will likely integrate genomic variation with dynamic measures of autophagic flux, lysosomal competence, mitochondrial quality control, and immune-metabolic state. Candidate intervention classes already exist, including mTOR inhibitors, AMPK activators, caloric-restriction mimetics, spermidine, and emerging lysosome-targeted agents, but their clinical deployment will require attention to dose, timing, and contraindications such as cachexia, infection risk, or tumor context ref [208], ref [429], ref [430], ref [431], ref [432]. In oncology especially, autophagy can suppress malignant initiation yet sustain established tumors under therapeutic stress, making patient selection and combination design essential ref [220], ref [433].

A realistic future priority is therefore prevention-oriented longitudinal profiling: identifying individuals in whom declining proteostasis, inflammaging, or metabolic inflexibility signals an autophagy-responsive trajectory before irreversible pathology emerges. Progress will depend on validated blood- and imaging-based biomarkers, single-cell and spatial readouts, and adaptive trials that test whether restoring autophagic fitness improves resilience rather than only late-stage disease endpoints ref [14], ref [434].
